terms.comment: The ordinary word of classical prose; Lewis & Short finds āctūtum above all in Plautus, and hardly in classical prose.

evidence: Plaut. Bacch. 3.1.7: quae ut aspexī, mē continuō contulī (Lewis & Short s.v. continuus)
terms.comment: What follows straight on something else: “very frequent in all periods”, Lewis & Short.

evidence: Lewis & Short s.v. nunc, referring to jam
terms.comment: Traupman prints nunciam; with consonantal j the house spelling is nuncjam. Lewis & Short has no entry of its own for the word and sends the reader to jam.

evidence: Lewis & Short s.v. prōtinus: immediately, at once

terms.register: vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut., Ter.; et in historiīs

phrases.latin: «Agedum,» inquit pater, «onerā palliolō umerōs tuōs, et āctūtum sequere mē.»
phrases.english: “Come on,” said Dad, “put your little coat on your shoulders and follow me at once.”
phrases.source: Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus

sources: Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 7 November 2026, with their glosses. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word; classical passages are cited by author.
Lewis & Short: statim. John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 87.
Lewis & Short: continuo · Lewis & Short: nunc
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency (printed page numbers): p. 331.
